big_idea: Counting things in groups gives us DATA — numbers we can use.
learning_intention: We are learning to collect data by counting things in groups.
student_learning_goal: I can collect data by counting things in groups.
success_criteria: I can count items in a group.
I can record the count on a tally chart.
I can collect data for 3+ groups.
lesson_specific_materials: OPTIONAL: Detective Dot and Tally — if available; otherwise teacher voices both characters in two distinct voices, or substitutes two stuffed animals / paper-bag puppets / pictures on the anchor poster. Activity is unaffected.
Lesson 2 counting tracker — provided in assessment_suite stage

minds_on.hook: Detective Dot sorted the buttons. Tally COUNTS them.
minds_on.teacher_script:
Bring children to the carpet. Detective Dot + Tally puppets. 'Friends — yesterday Detective Dot sorted. Today Tally COUNTS each group. We get DATA.'

Introduce vocabulary. Write DATA on chart. 'Data is numbers we get by COUNTING. Each group has a count.'

Demonstrate. Show sorted buttons (red, blue, yellow, green from yesterday). Tally counts. 'Red: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8. Eight reds.' Make 8 tally marks on chart.

More counts: 'Blue: 5. Yellow: 7. Green: 4.' Total marks. 24 buttons total.

Introduce tally chart format. Five marks = a bundle (||||̸).

More examples:
- Children's eye colour: brown 12, blue 5, green 3.
- Lunch boxes: red 8, blue 6, plain 4.
- Snowflakes vs raindrops collected.

'Tally says — count each group ONCE. Don't double count. Mark each item once.'

'Today we sort and COUNT. Tally chart for each group.'

steps.instruction: Whole group: count 4 sorted button groups. Tally each. Total all.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say: 'Tally each group. One mark per item.'

steps.instruction: Three stations. Station A: Count Buttons. Station B: Count Mixed Objects. Station C: Class Survey — pair surveys 6 classmates' favourite colour.
Stretch challenge at Station C: count more classmates and total.
Discuss tally marks. 'Bundle by 5s. Easy to count.'
steps.teacher_prompt: Show data anchor chart: tally examples.

steps.instruction: Circulate to record formative evidence on the counting tracker.
steps.teacher_prompt: Stop at each pair. Mark the tracker.

steps.instruction: Two pairs share their counts of the same set. Compare totals; if different, find the over-count or under-count. Cite CGI counting research.
steps.teacher_prompt: Detective Dot: 'Different paths, same goal. Math says: try multiple ways!'

differentiation.for_extending: Stretch at Station C: more classmates.
differentiation.for_movement_learners: Walk around classroom counting things by attribute. NO-PAPER PATH: children tally on fingers as teacher names items; switch hands every 5.

formative_check.what_to_look_for: Three signals: counts each group; tallies accurately; collects data for 3+ groups.

consolidation.exit_routine: Detective Dot's refrain — class chants 3x: 'Tally's rule: ONE touch, ONE tally!' Each child writes one finding on a sticky.

expanded_walkthrough.title: When the child double-counts items — repairing the count-twice trap at K
expanded_walkthrough.rationale:
On counting data, K trap is one-to-one correspondence lapse — child counts faster than they touch (Sarama & Clements 2009; CGI counting). Today: ONE touch ONE tally. Lesson 3 graphs; Lesson 4 likelihood; Lesson 5 capstones.

The most common K trap on A8.2 is the double-count: child counts the same item twice, getting an inflated total. They miss that each item gets ONE tally.

This matters because data accuracy depends on one-to-one counting.

The walkthrough covers when child counts a button twice.
expanded_walkthrough.setup: Pair is at Station A. 8 red buttons. Child counts 'one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten' and writes 10 tally marks.
expanded_walkthrough.teacher_script:
Crouch. 'Let's check. Count again, but TOUCH each button as you count.'

Touch button 1: 'one'. Touch button 2: 'two'. ...Touch button 8: 'eight'. 'There are 8 reds. Not 10.'

Generalise. 'Tally says — TOUCH each item ONCE as you count. Each touch = 1 tally.'

If still double-counting: have child move counted items to a separate pile. 'Counted ones go HERE.' Force separation.

Long-term recovery: every count uses touch-and-move technique.
expected_student_responses: (Strong) Touches and counts each item once.
(Stretched) Counts in bundles of 5; uses tally bundles.
common_misconceptions: Counting is fast. (Repair: counting is one-to-one.)
I can count without touching. (Repair: touch helps prevent doubles.)
Bigger numbers are estimates. (Repair: count exactly with touch.)
recovery_moves: DIAGNOSTIC A — child counts ahead of touching: drill 'point THEN say'; child slows to one tap per number.
DIAGNOSTIC B — child loses count past 5: chunk in groups of 5 with cross-tallies.
DIAGNOSTIC C — child counts but cannot record: drill 'COUNT-tally-COUNT-tally' rhythm.

parts_outline.task: Count things in your classroom by colour.
Class survey: tally favourite colour from 6 classmates.
